::: {.lead}
The update of *Torch Hall* adds a golden torch that drops from bats with a
chance of 5 %. Some players get it after three bats, others after a
hundred, and a few write angry reviews. The forum is full of posts: "My hit
chance is 70 % and I missed three times in a row: the game cheats!" The
team checks the code: the random numbers are fine. **Game balance** is the
work of setting such numbers so that the game is fair, challenging and fun,
and of making it **feel** fair. In lectures 10–11 you learned probability,
expected value and random numbers. In this lesson you **use** them: drop
rates, pity timers, rewards, streaks, the way players feel chance, and
shuffle bags. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-balance drop-rate pity-timer expected-value streak gamblers-fallacy hot-hand-fallacy perceived-probability independent-events critical-hit drought shuffle-bag >}}

## 12.1 Drop rates and "at least once"

A **drop rate** is the probability that one try gives the item. Players care
about another number: the chance to have it after their tries (@fig-least).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.1 — At least one drop in n tries"}
With drop rate p per try and independent tries,
$$P(\text{at least one in } n) = 1 - (1 - p)^n.$$
The complement "none in n tries" is (1 − p)ⁿ (lecture 10). The average
number of tries is 1/p (lecture 10).
:::

![Drop rate 5 %: the chance to have the torch after n bats.](images/at-least-one.png){#fig-least width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.1 — The golden torch"}
The golden torch drops from a bat with p = 0.05.

1. After 2 bats: none is 0.95 × 0.95 ≈ 0.90, so at least one is about
   **0.10**, not 0.05 + 0.05 exactly.
2. For many bats, read @fig-least: about **50 %** after 14 bats and **90 %**
   after 45 bats.
3. The average is 1/0.05 = 20 bats, but 10 % of the players need more than
   45: the designer must think about them.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"5 % per bat, so after 20 bats it is 100 %." Chances of independent tries do
not add up; use the complement.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Chances of a drop"}
A pet drops with p = 0.5. Compute the chance to have it after 1, 2 and 3
tries.

*Your result:* three probabilities.

::: {.check}
1/2; 1 − (1/2)² = 3/4; 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8. The chance grows, but it never
reaches 1.
:::
:::

## 12.2 Pity timers

To protect unlucky players, many games add a **pity timer** (@fig-pity).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.2 — Pity timer"}
A **pity timer** changes the chance after many misses: the item is
**guaranteed** after N tries without it, or its chance **grows** with every
miss. The tries are no longer independent, and the longest wait is limited.
:::

![A pity timer.](images/pity-timer.png){#fig-pity width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.2 — A guarantee at 40"}
1. Torch with p = 5 % and a guarantee at bat 40.
2. Without the timer, about 13 % of the players would still wait after 39
   bats; with it, all have the torch at 40.
3. The average falls a little (from 20 to about 17 bats).
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
int missesSinceTorch = 0;
void OnBatKilled() {
    bool drop = Random.value < 0.05f || missesSinceTorch >= 39;
    if (drop) { GiveTorch(); missesSinceTorch = 0; }
    else missesSinceTorch++;
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Hiding a very low drop rate behind a pity timer and calling it "5 %". Be
honest with players about how drops work; many stores require shown odds for
paid random items.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Pity"}
Read the pity timer of @fig-pity: after how many misses does the chance
start to grow? At which try is the item certain? What is the longest wait?

*Your result:* three numbers.

::: {.check}
After 20 misses (2 % per try before that); certain at try 40; so nobody
waits more than 40 tries.
:::
:::

## 12.3 Rewards: expected value and the economy

The expected value of rewards controls how fast players get rich (lecture
14).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.3 — Expected reward"}
For a chest with rarities of weight wᵢ and value vᵢ, the **expected reward**
is E = Σ vᵢ · wᵢ / Σ wᵢ. Compare E with the prices in the shop: if a sword
costs 300 coins and a chest gives 15 on average, a player needs about 20
chests for the sword.
:::

![The expected value of a loot crate (lecture 10).](../week-11/images/expected-value.png){#fig-ev width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.3 — The chest and the shop"}
Common 60 (5 coins), rare 30 (20 coins), epic 10 (60 coins):

1. E = 0.6·5 + 0.3·20 + 0.1·60 = 3 + 6 + 6 = **15 coins**.
2. A sword for 300 coins needs about 300 / 15 = 20 chests.
3. Too slow? Raise the rare value to 30: E = 18, about 17 chests.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Balancing with the plain average of the values ((5 + 20 + 60) / 3 ≈ 28):
the game then gives far fewer coins than planned.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The economy"}
A chest: 70 % gives 10 coins, 25 % gives 40 coins, 5 % gives 200 coins.
Compute E and the number of chests for a shield of 270 coins.

*Your result:* E and a number of chests.

::: {.check}
E = 7 + 10 + 10 = 27 coins; 270 ÷ 27 = 10 chests on average.
:::
:::

## 12.4 Real randomness is streaky

Ask a person to write 50 "random" coin flips, and the result changes from
heads to tails much too often. Real randomness has **long streaks**
(@fig-streaks).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.4 — Streaks in independent tries"}
A **streak** (or run) is a series of equal results in a row. For independent
tries with probability $p$ of a result, the chance of $k$ of them in a row
**at one given place** is $p^k$. But in a long sequence there are many
places where a streak can start, so **some** long streak is very likely.
In 100 fair coin flips, the longest run is about 7 on average, and a run of
5 or more appears in about 97 % of the sequences.
:::

![A person's sequence and a real coin.](images/streaks.png){#fig-streaks width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.4 — Three misses in a row"}
The guard hits with $p = 0.7$, so a miss has probability 0.3.

1. Three misses at one given place: $0.3^3 = 0.027$, about 2.7 %.
2. In a fight of 100 attacks there are almost 100 places to start, so a
   run of 3 misses somewhere is almost certain (a simulation shows it).
3. So the angry post describes something normal: rare at one place, common
   in a long game.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/streak-lab.html" poster="sims/streak-lab.png" title="Streak Lab: does random look random?" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"A run of 5 tails means the coin is not fair." In 100 flips a run of 5 is
expected. Judge fairness by many tries (the share of heads), not by one
streak.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Streaks"}
1. Write 50 "random" H and T on paper without a coin. Find your longest
   run.
2. In **Streak Lab**, run 100 attacks at 50 % five times. Compare the
   longest runs with yours.

*Your result:* your longest run and five computer runs.

::: {.check}
Most people write runs of only 2 or 3 and change too often. The computer
runs at 50 % are usually 5 to 8 long: real randomness is streakier than it
feels.
:::
:::

## 12.5 The gambler's fallacy and the hot hand

Players often believe that the past changes the next random result
(@fig-memory).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.5 — Two fallacies"}
For **independent events**, $P(A \mid \text{any past results}) = P(A)$.

- The **gambler's fallacy:** "Tails came 4 times, so heads is **due**."
  Wrong: $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{1}{2}$ on every flip.
- The **hot-hand fallacy:** "I hit twice, so I am lucky now and will hit
  again." Wrong for independent tries.

Do not mix up the chance of a **whole sequence** with the chance of the
**next** result: $P(\text{TTTTH}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 = \frac{1}{32}$,
but $P(\text{H} \mid \text{TTTT}) = \frac{1}{2}$.
:::

![The coin has no memory.](images/no-memory.png){#fig-memory width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.5 — Two golden torches"}
The golden torch drops with $p = 0.05$ per bat.

1. A player gets the torch from bat 7 and then again from bat 8. The post
   says: "Two in a row! The drop is broken."
2. Two drops in a row at one place: $0.05^2 = 0.0025$. With 10,000 players
   who kill many bats, this happens to many of them every day.
3. After a drop, the next bat still has $p = 0.05$: the code has no memory,
   unless the designers add one (section 12.7).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Coding the gambler's fallacy by accident: "if the player missed, roll
again" changes the real chance. If you want memory, design it on purpose
and compute the new probabilities.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Due or not?"}
For each sentence, say "fallacy" or "correct" and give the probability:
(a) "After 3 misses at 70 %, the next attack is sure to hit."
(b) "The chance of 3 misses in a row at 70 % is less than 3 %."
(c) "I got a crit, so the next one will be a crit too."

*Your result:* three answers with probabilities.

::: {.check}
(a) Fallacy: the next attack still hits with 0.7. (b) Correct: 0.3³ =
0.027, less than 3 %. (c) Fallacy (hot hand): the next crit has the same
chance as before.
:::
:::

## 12.6 How players feel probabilities

The chance on the screen and the chance in the player's head are often
different (@fig-felt).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.6 — Perceived probability"}
The **perceived probability** is how likely a result feels. Studies of
players and the experience of designers show:

- High chances feel **sure**: a miss at 90 % feels like a bug.
- Players remember **bad streaks** more than good ones.
- Over many tries, rare results become likely:
  $P(\text{at least one miss in } n) = 1 - p^n$ for hit chance $p$.

Designers therefore test how a chance **feels** in a real fight, not only
the formula.
:::

![A high chance still misses.](images/felt-chance.png){#fig-felt width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.6 — The 90 % miss"}
1. The player attacks 10 times per fight with $p = 0.9$.
2. The table in @fig-felt gives $P(\text{at least one miss}) \approx 0.65$
   for 10 attacks at 90 %.
3. In 65 % of the fights the player sees a "90 % miss". Some strategy games
   secretly raise high chances for the player; *Torch Hall* chooses an
   honest way instead: it shows the last attacks and uses a shuffle bag
   for crits.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking "the numbers are right, so the players are wrong". A game is made
for people: if a fair rule feels unfair, the rule or the way you show it
needs work.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Feel the chance"}
Hit chance 90 %: compute $P(\text{at least one miss})$ in 2 attacks by
hand, then read 5 and 20 attacks in @fig-felt. Would a player feel 90 % as
"sure"?

*Your result:* three probabilities and one sentence.

::: {.check}
2 attacks: 1 − 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.19. 5 attacks: 41 %; 20 attacks: 88 %. No: in
a long fight a miss is very likely, but players feel 90 % as "sure".
:::
:::

## 12.7 Shuffle bags

A **shuffle bag** turns "25 % on average" into "exactly 1 in every 4"
(@fig-bag).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 12.7 — Shuffle bag"}
Put a fixed set of results into a bag, for example 1 crit and 3 normal
hits. Draw them in a **shuffled** order **without putting them back**. When
the bag is empty, refill and shuffle it again. The share of each result is
exact for every full bag, and the longest drought is limited: with 1 crit
in a bag of $n$, at most $2(n - 1)$ attacks in a row are without a crit.
The draws are **not independent** any more: that is the point.
:::

![A shuffle bag.](images/shuffle-bag.png){#fig-bag width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 12.7 — The crit bag"}
1. Bag of 4: 1 crit, 3 normal. In 100 attacks: exactly 25 crits.
2. The worst case: the crit is first in one bag and last in the next, so 6
   normal hits come between them.
3. With pure random 25 %, much longer droughts appear in many fights (Bag
   Lab shows them).
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
List<bool> bag = new List<bool>();
bool NextIsCrit() {
    if (bag.Count == 0) {
        bag.AddRange(new[] { true, false, false, false });
        for (int i = bag.Count - 1; i > 0; i--) {      // Fisher–Yates shuffle
            int j = Random.Range(0, i + 1);
            (bag[i], bag[j]) = (bag[j], bag[i]);
        }
    }
    bool crit = bag[bag.Count - 1];
    bag.RemoveAt(bag.Count - 1);
    return crit;
}
```
:::

{{< sim file="sims/bag-lab.html" poster="sims/bag-lab.png" title="Bag Lab: pure random or a shuffle bag?" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A bag that is too predictable. With a bag of 4, a careful player knows that
after a crit at the end of a bag, the next one comes within 4 attacks.
Larger bags (for example 2 crits in 8) feel more random but allow longer
droughts.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Bags"}
1. In **Bag Lab**, compare pure random and the shuffle bag over 1000
   players: the crit rate and the worst drought.
2. Compute the longest drought for a bag of 8 with 2 crits.

*Your result:* four numbers from the lab and one computed drought.

::: {.check}
Both give a crit rate close to 25 %, but the worst drought of pure random is
much longer (often 20 or more) than with the bag (6). A bag of 8 with 2
crits: both crits first in one bag and last in the next: 6 + 6 = **12**.
:::
:::

## Case study: Fair or Frustrating?

The *Torch Hall* team reads six messages. A player hits with 80 % and
missed two times in a row. Another rolled no 6 in five rolls and thinks a 6
is "due". A third hits with 70 % and missed once in two attacks. A key
drops with 50 %, and a player tried three times. Crits come with 20 %, and
the team tries a shuffle bag with 1 crit and 4 normal hits. A chest gives
10 coins (80 %) or 50 coins (20 %), and a bow costs 180 coins. The Game
challenge of the interactive page uses these messages. In the mini-game
below you answer each one with probability and the tools of today.

{{< sim file="sims/fair-or-frustrating.html" poster="sims/fair-or-frustrating.png" title="Fair or Frustrating? Messages about luck" kind="game" height="440" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., Chapter 12 (chance and
balance). Rabin (ed.), *Game AI Pro* (2013), Chapter 3 "Advanced Randomness
Techniques for Game AI".

## Exercises

1. A rare fish bites with p = 0.5 per cast. P(at least one in 2 casts)?
2. Why is "10 % per try, so 100 % after 10 tries" wrong?
3. A pity timer guarantees a drop at try 30. What is the longest wait?
4. Why do many games show the odds of paid random items?
5. A chest: 50 % gives 4 coins, 50 % gives 16 coins. E? How many chests for
   a hat of 100 coins?
6. Why is the plain average of the values wrong for a chest?
7. Hit chance 60 %. P(two misses in a row at one place)?
8. "Heads came 3 times, so tails is due." Name the fallacy and give the
   chance of tails.
9. "I hit twice, so I am hot now." Name the fallacy.
10. Hit chance 80 %, 2 attacks. P(at least one miss)?
11. A bag holds 1 crit and 2 normal hits. What is the crit rate? What is the
    longest wait without a crit?
12. Why are the draws of a shuffle bag not independent?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 1 − (1/2)² = 3/4.
2. The tries are independent: none in 10 is 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35, so at least one is
   only about 65 %.
3. 29 misses, then the drop at try 30.
4. So that players know the real chance before they pay (many stores
   require it).
5. E = 2 + 8 = 10 coins; about 10 chests.
6. The values have different probabilities.
7. 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16.
8. The gambler's fallacy; 1/2.
9. The hot-hand fallacy.
10. 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.36.
11. 1/3; 2 · (3 − 1) = 4 normal hits.
12. A drawn result does not go back: the next draw depends on what is left.
:::
